claim: Split conformal prediction wraps any pre-trained classifier to output label sets that contain the true label with a user-chosen probability, with finite-sample, distribution-free validity that rests on calibration and test data being exchangeable.
evidence: "sets that are guaranteed to contain the ground truth with a user-specified probability, such as 90%"; "explicit, non-asymptotic guarantees even without distributional assumptions or model assumptions"
plain: Instead of one guess, the model gives a short list of possible diseases and promises the right one is in the list, say, 90% of the time, as long as new photos look like the photos used to set it up.
project_use: Use split conformal on top of our trained classifier as the 'I'm not sure' mechanism: a set with more than one disease means defer to the expert; the guarantee only holds if the calibration photos come from the same distribution as deployment photos.

claim: APS (Romano et al. 2020) and RAPS (Angelopoulos et al. 2021) are the standard prediction-set scores for image classifiers; RAPS adds regularisation to keep sets small while preserving coverage.
evidence: APS: "prediction sets with guaranteed marginal coverage" and favourable "approximate conditional coverage"; RAPS: sets "often factors of 5 to 10 smaller" than a standalone Platt scaling baseline (ImageNet / ImageNet-V2 experiments)
plain: There are ready-made recipes for building these 'shortlists'; one (RAPS) is tuned to keep the shortlist short so it stays useful.
project_use: Compare APS vs RAPS (plus simple LAC/threshold score) on field photos, reporting both empirical coverage and average set size, since set size drives how many cases go to the expert.

claim: Weighted conformal prediction restores coverage under covariate shift by reweighting calibration points with the test/train likelihood ratio, which can be estimated from unlabelled target inputs.
evidence: "the test and training covariate distributions differ, but the likelihood ratio between these two distributions is known"; it "can be estimated accurately with access to a large set of unlabeled data (test covariate points)"
plain: If field photos differ from lab photos, you can give more weight to lab examples that look field-like, using unlabelled field photos to decide the weights.
project_use: Optional baseline: train a lab-vs-field domain classifier on unlabelled field photos to get weights; but lab-to-field is not pure covariate shift (labels and class mix also change), so treat it as a comparison, not the main fix.

claim: In medical imaging, conformal coverage breaks under input and label distribution shift, but recalibrating on about 1,000 labelled target-domain images restored the guarantee; it is also unreliable per-class and of limited value with few classes.
evidence: "under domain-shift the coverage guarantee is not upheld" (CAMELYON17, 90% target); "after re-calibrating on a subset of size 1000 of the Camelyon17 domain-shifted images, we again observe the coverage guarantees"; abstract: "not reliable for subsets of the data, such as individual classes"
plain: A medical study found the 90% promise silently failed on photos from new hospitals, and was only fixed by re-tuning on about 1,000 expert-labelled photos from the new hospital.
project_use: Directly frames our 'how many expert labels' question: run a sweep of target calibration sizes (e.g. 25-1000 field photos) and measure when lab-calibrated vs field-recalibrated coverage reaches 90%; also report per-class coverage.

claim: Adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs & Candes 2021) keeps long-run coverage under arbitrary, changing distribution shift by continually updating one threshold parameter online as labelled feedback arrives.
evidence: "provably achieves the desired coverage frequency over long-time intervals irrespective of the true data generating process"; "robust to visible and significant distribution shifts"
plain: Each time the expert confirms or corrects a case, the system nudges how cautious it is, so over time it keeps its 90% promise even as conditions change.
project_use: Natural fit for expert-in-the-loop: simulate a stream of field photos where each expert label updates the threshold; guarantee is long-run average, not per-photo, so state that limitation.

claim: In a real precision-weeding deployment, a conformalized image classifier kept 90% coverage on most farms under near out-of-distribution data, but coverage fell well below target on some farms.
evidence: certify spraying "at least 90% of the weeds"; near-OOD: "the coverage guarantee is maintained for most of the farms" but for Farm 20 and Farm 23 "the coverage is far from the required 90% level"
plain: On real farms, the safety promise mostly held but broke on a couple of farms that looked different from the training data.
project_use: Closest agricultural evidence: report coverage per field source/site, not just pooled, since site-level failures hide in averages.

claim: We found no peer-reviewed or arXiv paper (2023-2026) applying conformal prediction to crop disease image classification under lab-to-field shift; nearby agricultural work covers weeding, crop/weed and plant-species identification only.
evidence: Searches surfaced Melki et al. (weeding, arXiv 2501.07185), group-conditional CP for crop/weed (arXiv 2308.15094), Pl@ntNet species ID (arXiv 2507.07150); the weeding paper cites disease identification only via a general ML survey (Domingues et al. 2022, Agriculture 12(9):1350)
plain: Nobody seems to have tested whether these shortlist guarantees survive when a leaf-disease model trained on lab photos meets real field photos.
project_use: This is our novelty angle: first measurement of conformal coverage on lab-trained crop disease models evaluated on field photos, plus label budget for recalibration.
